Facility booking predictions

For a resident at a moment in time, every model predicts four things: which facility, which weekday, which hour, and how long until they book. The Records tab holds one row per model per record, beside what actually happened.

Showing the test split — 11,288 rows across 4 models. The holdout has been scored once, so this workbook renders it. Every row here was predicted before any holdout target was read, and the settings that produced it were frozen beforehand.

How a prediction is scored

Facility, weekday and hour are exact-match: the answer counts only if it names the right one. Notification is scored inside a ±25% window of the real delay, because it is a question about magnitude rather than about a minute.

The overall score is the mean of those four rates. The same number chose the model and leads the report, so no model can be picked on one measure and presented with a more flattering one.

Why the scores sit near a quarter

Most of what is predictable here is that residents repeat themselves, and the frequency/recency rule already captures it. A deliberately unfair reference — a lookup allowed to see each resident's whole history including the future — reaches only 0.3791 / 0.2732 / 0.2040 on facility / weekday / hour. The trained models match or exceed that, so they are at the ceiling of what habit alone can tell you.

Booking delay is the hardest of the four for every model: the gap to a resident's next booking carries almost no memory of the previous gap, and the whole winnable band is about five points wide.

Leakage controls

Every feature is computed from events at or before its row's prediction origin. Six numbered controls enforce that, asserted per row on every run rather than only in tests: resident history bounded by the origin, no target-derived column as an input, community windows closed strictly before the origin, a chronological split that cannot overlap, frozen split membership audited at every fit, and generator hidden state kept out of the modelling table.

Two further checks look for the effect of a leak: a future-perturbation property test, and a shuffled-label control. Both carry a sensitivity check, because an instrument that has gone blind passes everything.

Scored once, and reproducible

The holdout is scored once, ever. A freeze written before any holdout row is read and a seal written after make that enforced rather than intended; a second attempt is refused.

One seed drives the generator, the splits and every fit. make verify recomputes every committed value — digests, both splits' metrics, the workbook hash — and fails on any difference. This page is rendered from the same scored frame as the workbook, so the two cannot disagree.

What this page is not

It is a record-level view, not the result. Sampling the table until a model looks good is exactly the mistake the single-scoring rule exists to prevent. The headline figures are computed over every row on the selected split, and the full write-up lives in docs/REVIEW.md.
